document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 64-year-old man reports a 2-year history of urinary frequency, urgency and nocturia, together with a weak stream, hesitancy and post-void dribbling. He takes no medications and has never been catheterized or instrumented. Urinalysis shows no blood, leukocytes or nitrites. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, rubbery, symmetrically enlarged prostate with no nodules. No bladder is palpable suprapubically. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Neurogenic bladder due to a spinal cord lesion

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes benign prostatic hyperplasia as proliferation of epithelial tissue, connective tissue and smooth muscle in the prostatic transition zone, which is age-related and extremely common (50% of men aged 50, 80% of men aged 80). It produces both voiding symptoms (stream changes, straining, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, post-void dribbling) and storage symptoms (frequency, urgency, nocturia), and on digital rectal examination the prostate is smooth, rubbery and may be symmetrically enlarged. This patient's chronic symptom pattern and DRE findings fit that description exactly.

optionExplanations.b: Prostate cancer is suspected when the DRE is abnormal with nodularity or focal change in texture, not with a smooth symmetrically enlarged gland.
optionExplanations.c: Neurological causes of bladder dysfunction are suggested by reduced anal sphincter tone, abnormal reflexes or saddle anesthesia, none of which are present.
optionExplanations.d: Acute retention is characterized by suprapubic pain and an inability to void with a palpable or percussible bladder; this man is voiding and has no palpable bladder.
optionExplanations.e: Infection is unlikely with a bland urinalysis showing no pyuria or nitrites and no purulent meatal discharge.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep. He has vomited twice. The left testis is diffusely tender, retracted and lies horizontally in the scrotum. The cremasteric reflex is absent on that side and elevating the testis does not relieve the pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Immediate urological consultation for emergency scrotal exploration and bilateral orchiopexy
Obtain a Doppler ultrasound and proceed only if arterial flow is absent
Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline for presumed epididymitis
Needle aspiration of the scrotal contents for diagnosis
Scrotal support, analgesia and reassessment in 12 hours

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists acute onset of severe scrotal pain with a retracted, transverse (horizontal lie) testicle, an absent cremasteric reflex and a negative Prehn's sign as the features of testicular torsion, and notes that necrosis of testicular tissue occurs in 5-6 hours. The treatment is emergency surgical exploration with bilateral orchiopexy, and the text explicitly states that a definitive diagnosis is NOT necessary before taking the patient to the operating room.

optionExplanations.b: Doppler ultrasound is listed as an investigation, but waiting for imaging delays exploration in a presentation that is torsion until proven otherwise.
optionExplanations.c: Epididymitis is associated with epididymal rather than diffuse tenderness, a present cremasteric reflex and a positive Prehn's sign.
optionExplanations.d: Aspiration has no role in the acute scrotum and does not relieve the twist or restore perfusion.
optionExplanations.e: Observation risks irreversible ischemic necrosis, which occurs within hours of the onset of torsion.

source.reference: U32 — Benign Scrotal Masses / Testicular Torsion

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with stable angina taking isosorbide dinitrate and a nitroglycerin spray reports 8 months of inability to obtain an erection adequate for intercourse. Onset was gradual and morning erections are absent. He also has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia. He has stopped smoking, increased his physical activity and completed sexual counselling without benefit. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: Vacuum erection device with a constriction ring
Insertion of an inflatable penile prosthesis

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated in patients on nitrates or nitroglycerin because of severe hypotension, which rules out all oral agents in this man. Treatment is otherwise organized from non-invasive through minimally invasive to invasive and surgical options; the vacuum device, which draws blood into the penis by negative pressure with a ring placed at the base, is the appropriate minimally invasive choice once lifestyle change and counselling have failed.

optionExplanations.a: Sildenafil is a PDE5 inhibitor and is contraindicated with concurrent nitrate therapy.
optionExplanations.b: Tadalafil is also a PDE5 inhibitor and carries the same nitrate contraindication.
optionExplanations.d: Intracavernosal injection is an invasive option reserved for failure of non-invasive and minimally invasive measures, and risks priapism and tunical fibrosis.
optionExplanations.e: A penile implant is surgical management and is not offered before less invasive options have been tried.

questions.question: A 34-year-old previously healthy man presents with 3 days of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. He is afebrile with no costovertebral angle tenderness and no urethral discharge. He has no urological history, no indwelling catheter and takes no medications. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and bacteriuria, and urine culture is pending. Which of the following best classifies this patient's urinary tract infection?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies a urinary tract infection as uncomplicated only when it is a lower tract infection in a functionally and structurally normal urinary tract, and lists male patients explicitly among the complicated categories, alongside structural or functional abnormality, immunocompromise, diabetes, iatrogenic complication, pregnancy, pyelonephritis and catheter-associated infection. Male sex alone therefore makes this a complicated UTI even though the tract is otherwise normal.

optionExplanations.a: Asymptomatic bacteriuria requires an absence of symptoms with 100,000 CFU/mL; this man has dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain.
optionExplanations.b: The uncomplicated category is reserved for lower tract infection in a functionally and structurally normal tract, and does not apply to male patients.
optionExplanations.d: Recurrent infection is defined by repeated episodes, and this is his first presentation.
optionExplanations.e: Pyelonephritis would be suggested by fever and costovertebral angle tenderness, both of which are absent.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man presents with the abrupt onset of severe right flank pain that waxes and wanes and radiates to the right testis. He is writhing on the stretcher, unable to find a comfortable position, and is nauseated, vomiting, diaphoretic and tachycardic. He is afebrile and the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes urinary obstruction causing upstream distention and pain, with severe waxing and waning pain radiating from flank to groin, testis or tip of penis, accompanied by writhing persistent discomfort, nausea, vomiting, hematuria (microscopic in 90%), diaphoresis, tachycardia and tachypnea. This constellation, in an afebrile patient with a soft abdomen and microscopic hematuria, is classic ureteral colic.

optionExplanations.b: Pyelonephritis is in the differential of renal colic, but fever would be expected and its presence should prompt evaluation for concurrent infection and obstruction.
optionExplanations.c: Abdominal aortic aneurysm is listed in the differential of renal colic but typically presents in an older patient with hemodynamic compromise rather than colicky pain with hematuria.
optionExplanations.d: Appendicitis is one of the other acute abdominal crises in the differential, but it produces localized abdominal tenderness rather than a soft non-tender abdomen.
optionExplanations.e: Neuromuscular back pain does not produce colicky pain radiating to the testis with nausea, vomiting and hematuria.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman has had four culture-proven urinary tract infections with Proteus mirabilis in the past year and reports dull right flank discomfort. Repeated urine dipsticks show a persistently alkaline pH and positive cultures. Non-contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrates a large branched calculus occupying the right renal pelvis and extending into several calyces. Which of the following is the most likely stone composition?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones result from infection with urea-splitting organisms such as Proteus, Pseudomonas, Providencia, Klebsiella, Mycoplasma, Serratia and S. aureus, which produce an alkaline urinary pH and precipitation of struvite. These stones perpetuate urinary tract infection because the stone itself harbours the organism, and they are associated with staghorn calculi, exactly as seen in this branched calculus with recurrent Proteus infection.

optionExplanations.b: Calcium stones are the most common overall but arise from metabolic abnormalities such as hypercalciuria and are not driven by urea-splitting infection or alkaline urine.
optionExplanations.c: Uric acid stones precipitate in low-volume acidic urine with a pH below 5.5, the opposite of this patient's persistently alkaline urine.
optionExplanations.d: Cystine stones can be staghorn in shape but reflect an autosomal recessive transport defect presenting with aggressive stone disease in children and young adults with a family history.
optionExplanations.e: Calcium phosphate is a recognized stone type, but the combination of urea-splitting Proteus infection and a staghorn configuration points to struvite.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with tuberous sclerosis undergoes CT of the abdomen for vague right-sided discomfort. A 2 cm right renal lesion is identified that contains areas of negative attenuation measuring approximately -20 Hounsfield units. She has no hematuria, no palpable mass, normal renal function and no weight loss. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes the angiomyolipoma (renal hamartoma) as a clonal neoplasm of blood vessels, smooth muscle and fat that is usually an incidental finding on CT, with negative attenuation of about -20 HU being pathognomonic. Approximately 20% are associated with tuberous sclerosis, particularly when multiple or recurrent, which matches this patient's background and imaging.

optionExplanations.b: Oncocytoma is also found incidentally on CT but is difficult to distinguish from renal cell carcinoma on imaging and does not show fat attenuation.
optionExplanations.c: Renal cell carcinoma may present incidentally, but negative fat attenuation is not a feature and it is not linked to tuberous sclerosis.
optionExplanations.d: A simple cyst is a fluid-density lesion and would not contain macroscopic fat.
optionExplanations.e: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma presents with hematuria and a filling defect rather than a fat-containing parenchymal lesion.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history reports two episodes of painless gross hematuria in the past month. He has no fever, flank pain or voiding symptoms. Urinalysis confirms hematuria with no red cell casts and no dysmorphic red cells, and urine culture is negative. CT with contrast of the abdomen and pelvis shows no upper tract filling defect or mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum and urinary bladder tumour markers such as NMP-22

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that the entire urinary tract must be evaluated in patients with hematuria unless there is clear evidence of glomerular bleeding such as red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, and that unexplained hematuria in anyone over 40 must be investigated to rule out malignancy. Cystoscopy is identified as the initial procedure of choice for the diagnosis and staging of urothelial malignancy, so a negative upper tract CT does not end the workup.

optionExplanations.b: Deferring investigation is unsafe because unexplained hematuria over the age of 40 must be investigated to exclude malignancy.
optionExplanations.c: Renal biopsy targets glomerular disease, which is excluded here by the absence of red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells.
optionExplanations.d: The clinical utility of bladder tumour markers such as NMP-22, BTA, Immunocyt and FDP is described as debatable and they do not replace cystoscopy.
optionExplanations.e: Proteinuria quantification investigates glomerular pathology, which is not suggested by this bland non-glomerular hematuria.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man presents with an episode of acute urinary retention and is relieved by urethral catheterization. A prostate specific antigen level drawn the same day is reported as elevated. After the catheter is removed and he is voiding normally, digital rectal examination is smooth with no nodularity or asymmetry. He has no bone pain, no weight loss and no family history of prostate cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the PSA once the retention has resolved and the catheter has been out for a period of time
Proceed directly to transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy
Order a bone scan to look for skeletal metastases
Advise that no further PSA testing is required

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes emphasizes that PSA is specific to the prostate but not to prostate cancer, and lists acute urinary retention and urethral catheterization among the recognized causes of an increased PSA, along with BPH, prostatitis, prostate biopsy or surgery, prostatic massage, cystoscopy, TRUS, strenuous exercise, perineal trauma and ejaculation. With a benign DRE and two active confounders, the appropriate step is to repeat the measurement once those confounders have resolved.

optionExplanations.b: Biopsy is driven by a genuinely suspicious PSA or abnormal DRE; committing to it on a confounded value risks unnecessary intervention.
optionExplanations.c: Bone imaging is reserved for bone pain, high-risk disease or markedly elevated PSA, none of which is established here.
optionExplanations.d: Hormonal therapy is treatment for advanced or metastatic disease and there is no tissue diagnosis.
optionExplanations.e: Abandoning follow-up ignores that the elevation may persist and still require evaluation once confounders are removed.

source.reference: U28 — PSA Screening, Causes of Increased PSA

questions.question: A 68-year-old man is referred after an abnormal screening test and is found on transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy to have prostate adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 9. His PSA is 28 ng/mL and digital rectal examination suggests extension beyond the capsule. He denies bone pain. CT of the abdomen and pelvis and multiparametric prostate MRI have already been completed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serial PSA measurements to calculate PSA velocity
Plain radiographs of the pelvis and lumbar spine

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists bone scan as part of the investigation of prostate cancer only if there is bone pain, high-risk disease, a Gleason score above 7, or a PSA above 20 ng/mL. This man satisfies three of those criteria (Gleason 9, PSA 28 ng/mL and high-risk disease with apparent extracapsular extension), so a bone scan is indicated even though he is asymptomatic, and the cross-sectional imaging he has already had does not substitute for it.

optionExplanations.b: The tissue diagnosis and grade are already established; repeating the biopsy adds nothing to staging.
optionExplanations.c: Prostate cancer spreads to the axial skeleton as bony metastases detected by bone scan, not by marrow sampling.
optionExplanations.d: PSA velocity is associated with cancer detection rates rather than being a staging investigation in established high-risk disease.
optionExplanations.e: Plain films are insensitive for skeletal metastases compared with the bone scan specified for these high-risk criteria.

questions.question: Ninety minutes into a monopolar transurethral resection of the prostate performed under spinal anesthesia with glycine irrigation, a 72-year-old man becomes confused and nauseated and vomits. He complains of blurred vision. Blood pressure is 172/95 mmHg and heart rate is 52 beats/min. Crackles are audible at both lung bases and serum sodium is low. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes transurethral resection syndrome as absorption of a large volume of the hypotonic glycine irrigation solution, usually through perforated venous sinusoids, producing a hypervolemic hyponatremic state. It is characterized by dilutional hyponatremia, confusion, nausea, vomiting, hypertension, bradycardia, visual disturbances, congestive heart failure and pulmonary edema, and is treated with diuresis and, if severe, hypertonic saline. The syndrome does not occur with bipolar TURP because saline irrigation is used.

optionExplanations.b: Hemorrhage is a recognized acute complication of TURP but would cause hypotension and tachycardia rather than hypertension with bradycardia and hyponatremia.
optionExplanations.c: Sepsis is a listed complication but typically produces fever and hypotension, not the dilutional hyponatremia and volume overload seen here.
optionExplanations.d: Bladder rupture is described as a rare complication and would present with abdominal pain and peritonism rather than hyponatremia and pulmonary edema.
optionExplanations.e: Myocardial infarction does not explain the low serum sodium, visual disturbance and hypervolemic picture that follow hypotonic irrigant absorption.

source.reference: U46 — Transurethral Resection of the Prostate, Complications

questions.question: A 27-year-old man presents with a painless, firm right testicular mass noted on self-examination. Scrotal ultrasound shows a hypoechoic area within the tunica albuginea. Serum AFP, beta-hCG and LDH are all elevated. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy or visceral lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Radical orchiectomy through an inguinal incision with ligation of the spermatic cord in the inguinal canal
Trans-scrotal incisional biopsy of the mass
Percutaneous needle aspiration of the lesion for cytology
Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection before any testicular surgery
Observation with repeat tumour markers and ultrasound in 3 months

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that the diagnosis of testicular cancer is established by pathological evaluation of the specimen obtained by radical inguinal orchiectomy, and that radical orchiectomy through an inguinal incision with ligation of the spermatic cord inside the inguinal canal is performed for all stages. A hypoechoic area within the tunica albuginea on ultrasound carries a high suspicion of testicular cancer, so this man needs orchiectomy rather than any lesser diagnostic manoeuvre; sperm banking and a prosthesis should also be discussed.

optionExplanations.b: The testes and scrotum have different lymphatic drainage, so a trans-scrotal approach for biopsy or orchiectomy should be avoided.
optionExplanations.c: Needle aspiration is contraindicated because of the risk of tumour seeding.
optionExplanations.d: Retroperitoneal surgery is not the initial procedure; the primary tumour is removed first and imaging here shows no retroperitoneal disease.
optionExplanations.e: Surveillance is inappropriate for a suspicious intratesticular mass with elevated tumour markers, which requires prompt orchiectomy for diagnosis.

source.reference: U30 — Testicular Tumours, Investigations and Management

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with three prior vaginal deliveries reports involuntary leakage of small amounts of urine whenever she coughs, sneezes, or lifts boxes at work. There is no preceding urge to void, no nocturia, and no dysuria. Urinalysis and urine culture are negative and post-void residual is 25 mL. A cough test reproduces the leakage. Which is the most likely type of urinary incontinence?

options.text: Stress incontinence from sphincter incompetence and urethral hypermobility
Overflow incontinence associated with urinary retention
Transient incontinence due to atrophic vaginitis

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines stress incontinence as leakage with sudden increases in intra-abdominal pressure (cough, sneeze, exertion), with sphincter incompetence and urethral hypermobility as the etiology, and it is common in middle-aged and older women. This patient leaks only with cough, sneeze, and exertion, has a positive cough test, and has no urgency and a low post-void residual, so the other patterns do not fit.

optionExplanations.b: Urgency incontinence is leakage preceded by a strong, sudden urge to void from detrusor overactivity or bladder hypersensitivity, which she does not describe.
optionExplanations.c: Mixed incontinence requires leakage with urgency as well as with increased intra-abdominal pressure; she has no urgency component.
optionExplanations.d: Overflow incontinence is leakage associated with urinary retention, which is excluded by a post-void residual of 25 mL.
optionExplanations.e: Atrophic vaginitis is a transient, reversible cause of incontinence in the elderly, but her leakage is provoked strictly by exertion and her examination and urinalysis are otherwise unremarkable.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man sustained a complete T6 spinal cord injury 8 months ago. He now has recurrent urinary tract infections and leaks between catheterizations. Urodynamic testing with electromyography demonstrates involuntary detrusor contractions occurring against a simultaneously contracting external sphincter, with high storage pressures and incomplete emptying. Which is the most likely form of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction?

options.text: Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia from a suprasacral spinal cord lesion
Neurogenic detrusor overactivity from a lesion above the pontine micturition centre
Detrusor atony/areflexia from a lesion of the sacral cord
Peripheral autonomic neuropathy with deficient bladder sensation
Muscular lesion of the detrusor and striated sphincter

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes attributes detrusor sphincter dyssynergia to a suprasacral lesion of the spinal cord, such as trauma, with loss of coordination between detrusor and sphincter so that the detrusor contracts on a closed sphincter, along with a component of detrusor overactivity. A complete T6 injury is suprasacral but below the pontine micturition centre, which produces exactly this uncoordinated pattern and the high storage pressures seen here.

optionExplanations.b: A lesion above the pontine micturition centre (stroke, tumour, MS, Parkinson's disease) causes loss of voluntary inhibition of voiding, but the pathway inferior to the centre keeps bladder and sphincter coordinated.
optionExplanations.c: Detrusor atony/areflexia follows a lesion of the sacral cord or peripheral nerves and gives a flaccid bladder that fails to contract, not involuntary detrusor contractions.
optionExplanations.d: Peripheral autonomic neuropathy, as in diabetes, causes deficient bladder sensation with increasing residual urine rather than sphincter contraction against a contracting detrusor.
optionExplanations.e: A muscular lesion of the detrusor or sphincter is not a consequence of spinal cord trauma and would not generate this coordinated-loss pattern.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man presents with a tender distended bladder and a creatinine of 320 micromol/L. A urethral catheter drains 1400 mL immediately. Over the next 6 hours he passes more than 300 cc of urine per hour and his serum sodium and potassium are falling. He is normotensive and tolerating oral intake poorly. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit, monitor urine output q2 h and electrolytes q6-12 h, and replace every 1 mL of urine output with 0.5 mL of IV half normal saline
Replace urine output millilitre for millilitre with IV 5% dextrose in water
Replace urine output millilitre for millilitre with IV normal saline
Withhold all fluid replacement and recheck creatinine in 24 hours as an outpatient
Give IV furosemide to maintain the diuresis

questions.explanation: Post-obstructive diuresis is polyuria of more than 3 L/24 h or more than 200 cc/h for two consecutive hours after relief of obstructive uropathy. Toronto Notes directs admission with close monitoring of hemodynamic status and of sodium and potassium q6-12 h, monitoring urine output q2 h, and ensuring total fluid intake is less than urine output by replacing every 1 mL of urine output with 0.5 mL of IV half normal saline. This man meets the volume criterion and has falling electrolytes, so he needs admission and controlled replacement rather than matched or absent replacement.

optionExplanations.b: Glucose-containing fluid replacement should be avoided because it causes an iatrogenic diuresis.
optionExplanations.c: Matching urine output millilitre for millilitre perpetuates the diuresis; total fluid intake must be kept below urine output.
optionExplanations.d: He is losing sodium and needs admission with electrolytes followed q6-12 h and creatinine and BUN followed to baseline; oral fluids alone are only adequate for physiologic post-obstructive diuresis.
optionExplanations.e: A diuretic worsens the sodium-wasting nephropathy that underlies pathologic post-obstructive diuresis.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man presents with 2 days of fever, chills, and malaise together with pelvic and perineal pain, urinary frequency, and dysuria. His temperature is 38.9 C. Digital rectal examination reveals an exquisitely tender prostate. Urinalysis shows pyuria and urine culture grows Escherichia coli. There is no flank pain and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies category I prostatitis as an acute infection, most often E. coli, presenting with LUTS and pelvic pain plus systemic signs of fever, chills, and malaise, with positive bacterial cultures. This man has exactly that combination with an acutely tender prostate, so category I acute bacterial prostatitis is the diagnosis.

optionExplanations.b: Chronic bacterial prostatitis produces LUTS, pelvic pain, and recurrent UTIs with no systemic signs, whereas this man is febrile and acutely unwell.
optionExplanations.c: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome is symptoms without evidence of infection; his urine culture is positive.
optionExplanations.d: Category IV is incidental inflammation with no symptoms, detected when investigating an elevated PSA or infertility.
optionExplanations.e: Acute pyelonephritis is a clinical diagnosis of flank pain, fever, and elevated WBC with CVA tenderness, which he does not have.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man develops 3 days of progressive left scrotal pain and swelling radiating along the cord to the flank, 2 weeks after cystoscopy and catheterization. He is febrile with scrotal erythema and tenderness, and his pain is relieved by lifting the testicle. Doppler ultrasound shows increased vascularity of the epididymis and a reactive hydrocele. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes divides the infectious causes of epididymitis by age: under 35 years the usual organisms are Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis, while at 35 years or older, or with penetrative anal intercourse, GI organisms, especially E. coli, predominate. Instrumentation and catheterization are listed risk factors, and this man's age, recent cystoscopy, Prehn's sign, increased vascularity on ultrasound, and reactive hydrocele all fit epididymitis from E. coli.

optionExplanations.b: Gonococcal infection is the typical cause in men under 35 years with unprotected sexual contact and purulent urethral discharge.
optionExplanations.c: Chlamydia is likewise the pathogen of the under-35 age group, not of post-instrumentation epididymitis in an older man.
optionExplanations.d: Tuberculosis is listed among other, uncommon causes and would present far more indolently.
optionExplanations.e: Syphilis is a rare listed cause and does not produce an acute febrile epididymitis after catheterization.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents with a painful rigid erection of 7 hours' duration that began in the absence of sexual excitement. There is no history of trauma. The corpora cavernosa are rigid and tender while the glans is soft, and cavernosal blood gas analysis confirms ischemic, low-flow priapism. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Needle aspiration and decompression of the corpora with intracorporeal phenylephrine injection q3-5 min
Observation with analgesia alone, as the episode is generally self-limited

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines priapism as a prolonged erection lasting more than 4 hours in the absence of sexual excitement and lists thromboembolic causes such as sickle cell disease among the ischemic forms. For low-flow priapism the treatment is needle aspirated decompression and intracorporeal phenylephrine injection q3-5 min, with a surgical shunt only if there is no response. This patient's confirmed ischemic priapism therefore calls for aspiration and phenylephrine first.

optionExplanations.b: Arterial embolization is considered for non-ischemic high-flow priapism, which is typically post-traumatic and often painless.
optionExplanations.c: A surgical shunt is reserved for cases that fail aspiration and intracorporeal phenylephrine.
optionExplanations.d: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated in men with a history of priapism or conditions predisposing to it, such as sickle cell disease.
optionExplanations.e: It is high-flow priapism that is generally self-limited; ischemic priapism risks necrosis and requires urgent decompression.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man and his partner have failed to conceive after 18 months of unprotected and properly timed intercourse. He reports learning difficulties and poor school performance as a child. Examination shows gynecomastia, sparse androgenic hair, and small, firm testes with palpable vas deferens bilaterally. Two semen analyses show azoospermia with a normal ejaculate volume of 3 mL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes the Klinefelter triad as small, firm testes, gynecomastia, and azoospermia, and notes that poor school performance or learning disabilities on social history is suggestive of Klinefelter syndrome. This man meets the definition of infertility, failure to conceive after 1 year of unprotected and properly timed intercourse, and has the full triad, making Klinefelter syndrome the best fit.

optionExplanations.b: Varicocele is the commonest testicular factor in infertile males but is found on Valsalva during scrotal exam and does not cause gynecomastia with small, firm testes.
optionExplanations.c: Congenital absence of the vas deferens, linked to CFTR mutation, is an obstructive cause and is excluded by palpable vas deferens bilaterally.
optionExplanations.d: Kallmann syndrome is a congenital hypothalamic hypogonadism affecting the HPT axis and would not produce this triad with normal-volume ejaculate.
optionExplanations.e: Retrograde ejaculation, secondary to surgery or medications, characteristically reduces ejaculate volume, which is normal here.

questions.question: A male neonate born at 38 weeks after a pregnancy complicated by oligohydramnios has a palpable abdominal mass from a distended bladder and a weak urinary stream. Prenatal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis, a thickened trabeculated bladder, and a dilated posterior urethra. He is now dehydrated with a rising creatinine. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Immediate catheterization to relieve the obstruction
Cystoscopic resection of the valves now
Antibiotic prophylaxis with repeat ultrasound in 3 months

questions.explanation: Posterior urethral valves are the most common congenital obstructive urethral lesion in male infants, recognized prenatally by bilateral hydronephrosis, a thickened and trabeculated bladder, a dilated posterior urethra, and oligohydramnios in a male fetus. Toronto Notes directs immediate catheterization to relieve the obstruction, followed by cystoscopic resection of the valves once the baby is stable. This unstable, dehydrated neonate therefore needs the catheter first.

optionExplanations.b: Cystoscopic resection follows catheterization and is done once the baby is stable, not while he is dehydrated with a rising creatinine.
optionExplanations.c: Vesicostomy is indicated only if resection of the valves is not possible.
optionExplanations.d: Ureteral reimplantation is a treatment for vesicoureteral reflux, not for the urethral obstruction causing his findings.
optionExplanations.e: Deferring drainage risks worsening renal insufficiency and urosepsis in an obstructed neonate.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man is brought to hospital after a motor vehicle collision. He has a pelvic fracture, has been unable to void for 6 hours, and has a distended bladder. Examination shows blood at the urinary meatus, a scrotal hematoma, and a high riding prostate on digital rectal examination. Bladder drainage and accurate monitoring of urine output are required. Which is the most appropriate method?

options.text: Insertion of a 16 Fr two-way Foley catheter per urethra
Insertion of a Coude tip catheter per urethra

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists blood at the urinary meatus, scrotal hematoma, pelvic fracture, and a high riding prostate as contraindications to catheterization in trauma, and gives suprapubic catheterization as the route when there is urethral disruption or obstruction. All four contraindications are present here, so the urethra must not be instrumented and a suprapubic catheter should be used to drain the bladder and monitor urine output.

optionExplanations.b: A standard transurethral Foley passed blindly through a disrupted urethra risks converting a partial injury into a complete one and is contraindicated by these findings.
optionExplanations.c: The Coude catheter has an angled tip to navigate around an enlarged prostate in BPH; it is still a transurethral catheter and is equally contraindicated.
optionExplanations.d: Intermittent catheterization is also transurethral and does not permit the accurate continuous monitoring of urine output required.
optionExplanations.e: A condom catheter cannot relieve retention or provide accurate urine output measurement.

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman reports 3 weeks of right flank pain and gross hematuria. CTU shows a filling defect in the right renal pelvis with hydronephrosis. Cystoscopy shows no bladder lesion, and retrograde pyelogram with biopsy confirms high grade urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis. Renal function is normal and there is no evidence of metastatic disease. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Radical nephroureterectomy with excision of the ipsilateral bladder cuff
Distal ureterectomy with concomitant ureteral reimplantation
Endoscopic laser ablation of the tumour
Radical cystectomy with ileal conduit urinary diversion

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes gives radical nephroureterectomy with excision of the ipsilateral bladder cuff as the treatment for urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis and ureter, reserving lesser resections for tumours confined to the ureter. This woman presents with the typical picture of gross hematuria, flank pain, and hydronephrosis with a filling defect, and her tumour is in the renal pelvis and high grade, so the whole upper tract unit plus the bladder cuff must be removed.

optionExplanations.b: Distal ureterectomy with concomitant ureteral reimplant is used for distal ureteral tumours, not for a tumour of the renal pelvis.
optionExplanations.c: Segmental resection with uretero-ureterostomy is an option for some mid-ureteral tumours only.
optionExplanations.d: Endoscopic laser ablation has an emerging role in patients with low grade disease and poor baseline renal health; her disease is high grade and her renal function is normal.
optionExplanations.e: Radical cystectomy treats bladder carcinoma, and cystoscopy showed no bladder lesion here.

source.reference: U24 — Carcinoma of the Renal Pelvis and Ureter

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is brought to hospital after a motor vehicle collision. He is alert, with blood pressure 124/78 mmHg and heart rate 88 bpm. He has left flank tenderness, a flank contusion, and a fractured left 11th rib. Urinalysis shows gross hematuria. Triphasic contrast CT shows a 0.6 cm renal laceration without urinary extravasation, no vascular injury, and no other intra-abdominal organ injury. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Hospitalization with bedrest, repeating CT if bleeding persists
Immediate surgical exploration of the injured kidney
Angiography with embolization of the injured kidney
Discharge without hospitalization, with repeat imaging at 6 wk

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that the majority of renal trauma is now managed conservatively and nonoperatively, with hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability the only absolute indication for surgical intervention. Microscopic hematuria with isolated well-staged minor injuries needs no hospitalization, whereas gross hematuria with a contusion or minor laceration is managed by hospitalization, bedrest, and repeat CT if bleeding persists. This man is hemodynamically stable with a <1 cm laceration and no urinary extravasation (stage II), so inpatient conservative management is appropriate.

optionExplanations.b: Surgical exploration is seldom necessary for contusions and superficial lacerations, which make up 90% of blunt renal trauma; the absolute indication is hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability, absent here.
optionExplanations.c: Angiography and embolization is reserved for relative indications such as vascular injury, an expanding or pulsating perirenal mass, or persistent bleeding, none of which is present.
optionExplanations.d: No hospitalization applies to microscopic hematuria with isolated well-staged minor injuries; this patient has gross hematuria and requires admission and bedrest.
optionExplanations.e: Laparotomy is a relative indication when there is an associated injury requiring it, but the CT shows no associated intra-abdominal organ injury.

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl is brought in after her mother felt a large, firm, painless left-sided abdominal mass while bathing her. Her blood pressure is well above the 99th percentile for age, and urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. Imaging confirms a renal tumour and also demonstrates a smaller tumour in the contralateral kidney; the renal vein contains no tumour thrombus. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Radical nephrectomy of the larger tumour with surveillance of the other kidney
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by nephron-sparing surgery
Radiation therapy alone to both kidneys
Nephron-sparing surgery on both kidneys followed by radiation alone

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes treats unilateral Wilms' tumour with radical nephrectomy or nephron-sparing surgery plus radiation and chemotherapy, but bilateral disease with nephron-sparing surgery following neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Bilateral involvement occurs in 5% of cases, which is why the contralateral kidney and renal vein must always be investigated. This child has the classic presentation of a large firm unilateral-appearing abdominal mass with HTN and microscopic hematuria, but imaging shows tumour in both kidneys, so chemotherapy precedes nephron-sparing resection.

optionExplanations.a: Removing both kidneys is not the described approach for bilateral disease; nephron-sparing surgery after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is used precisely to preserve renal tissue.
optionExplanations.b: Radical nephrectomy is the option for unilateral disease; leaving the contralateral tumour untreated ignores the bilateral involvement that must always be investigated.
optionExplanations.d: Radiation is given as part of combined therapy with surgery and chemotherapy, not as sole treatment.
optionExplanations.e: Bilateral disease requires neoadjuvant chemotherapy before nephron-sparing surgery; operating first without chemotherapy is not the described sequence.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman reports 10 months of urinary urgency, voiding more than 8 times in a 24 h period, and awakening twice each night to void. She has no leakage with coughing or lifting. Urinalysis rules out hematuria and infection, and post-void residual is normal. She drinks six cups of coffee daily. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Bladder training, fluid management, and avoidance of caffeine and alcohol

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists non-pharmacological behaviour therapies — bladder training, bladder control strategies, pelvic floor muscle training, fluid management, weight reduction, and avoidance of caffeine and alcohol — first in the treatment of overactive bladder, ahead of pharmacological agents, with botulinum toxin and neuromodulation reserved for refractory patients. This woman has the defining symptom complex of urgency, frequency of more than 8 voids in 24 h and nocturia, with urinalysis excluding hematuria and infection, so behavioural measures and reducing her caffeine intake are the appropriate first step.

optionExplanations.b: Solifenacin is one of the antimuscarinics listed under pharmacological treatment, which follows rather than replaces behaviour therapy.
optionExplanations.c: Mirabegron, a β3-adrenoceptor agonist, is also a pharmacological option rather than the initial treatment offered.
optionExplanations.d: Botulinum toxin bladder injection is listed for refractory patients, not for a newly assessed patient.
optionExplanations.e: Sacral neuromodulation is likewise reserved for refractory overactive bladder.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman reports 9 months of pelvic pain with suprapubic tenderness, together with urinary frequency, urgency, and nocturia. She has had no pelvic radiation and takes no ketamine or tiaprofenic acid. Urinalysis, urine culture, and urine cytology are all negative. Cystoscopy shows scattered submucosal petechiae without ulcerative lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines interstitial cystitis, or painful bladder/bladder pain syndrome, as bladder pain with chronic urgency and frequency without other identifiable causation, whose clinical features are pelvic pain with supra-pubic tenderness, storage symptoms, negative U/A, urine C&S and urine cytology, and cystoscopy showing glomerulations (submucosal petechiae) or Hunner's lesions. This 41-year-old woman fits the described epidemiology of a median age of 40 with 90% of cases in females, and the drug, radiation, and infectious entries on the differential have been excluded, leaving the non-ulcerative form.

optionExplanations.a: Overactive bladder appears on the urological differential and gives storage symptoms, but not the pelvic pain or the cystoscopic glomerulations.
optionExplanations.c: Bladder calculi are also on the urological differential, but cystoscopy showed submucosal petechiae rather than a stone.
optionExplanations.d: Radiation cystitis is one of the non-infectious cystitides listed, and is excluded by the absence of radiation exposure.
optionExplanations.e: Pudendal nerve entrapment is the neurological entry on the differential and would not produce glomerulations at cystoscopy.

source.reference: U15 — Interstitial Cystitis (Painful Bladder or Bladder Pain Syndrome)
